query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-homogenization aging treatment, designed to induce the formation of dual coherent nanoprecipitates (a sheared lamellar δ-phase combined with spheroidal γ″-particles), will mitigate dislocation pile-ups at the internal lamellar boundaries. This intervention will reduce local stress concentrations and microcracking, thereby increasing the room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or even enhancing the alloy’s high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies that currently exhibits limited tensile ductility and brittleness due to dislocation pile-ups at internal phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled short-duration high-temperature aging treatment after solution homogenization to precipitate dual coherent nanoprecipitates uniformly within the lamellae.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests (e.g., strain rate ~5×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹) under standard structural operating environments; microstructural analysis (TEM, EBSD) performed under similar conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dual coherent precipitate network consisting of δ-lamellae and nano-sized γ″ particles that interact with dislocations at internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coherent precipitates allow dislocation slip bands to shear the δ-lamellae without forming excessive stress concentrations, while the γ″ particles provide nanoscale obstacles to dislocation motion. Their synergy relieves dislocation pile-ups, thus delaying microcrack initiation and propagation during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in tensile ductility (targeting elongation to fracture in the 10–15% range or higher) accompanied by retention or enhancement of ultimate tensile strength (around or above 2 GPa), relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting brittle behavior with dislocation pile-ups, leading to premature microcracking and catastrophic failure at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under room-temperature tensile loading; effects under extreme strain rates, high temperatures, or long-term service conditions remain to be confirmed.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in ductility and strength depend on the specific aging parameters and subsequent microstructural evolution, which need experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the eutectic high-entropy alloy: one as the control (untreated) and one subjected to the controlled aging treatment designed to induce dual coherent nanoprecipitates. Characterize the microstructure of both sets using TEM and EBSD to confirm precipitate formation and distribution. Then, perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests to record stress–strain responses, focusing on ductility and strength. Additionally, use in-situ TEM to monitor dislocation behavior and pile-up at lamellar boundaries.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile stress–strain curves (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation to fracture)
TEM/EBSD assessment of precipitate coherence, size, and distribution
Observation and quantification of dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility (e.g., reaching at least 10–15% elongation) and/or if there is no measurable retention or enhancement of strength (approximately 2 GPa or higher) compared to the untreated samples, or if microstructural analysis shows no significant change in precipitate formation or dislocation behavior, the hypothesis will be falsified.
